Wilshire ran 32.5 years of options buy-write data. The 30-delta strike won the efficient frontier.

Not the at-the-money. Not the 2% OTM. The 30-delta.

Cboe BXMD Index (Wilshire Associates, 2019):

🔹 OWN S&P 500
🔹 SELL 1 CALL each month at approximately 0.30 delta (further OTM than BXM)
🔹 STRIKE ADAPTS to the implied vol regime monthly (Black-Scholes pricing)
🔹 LESS PREMIUM collected vs ATM, but you retain far more rally upside
🔹 MONTHLY REBALANCE, mechanical strike selection

Why the 30-delta beat both the ATM (BXM) and the 2% OTM (BXY) variants over 32.5 years: you give up a little premium cushion, but you keep enough upside that bull years stop being a drag.

This is what "mean-variance optimal" means in practice. Tune the strike, recover the upside, accept thinner downside buffer.

The takeaway for retail: the strike you pick matters more than whether you sell calls at all.

Here's proof that the strike you pick matters more than whether you sell calls.

Wilshire Associates ran 32.5 years of options buy-write data on the S&P 500. They compared three strikes:

🔹 The at-the-money call (BXM)
🔹 The 2% out-of-the-money call (BXY)
🔹 The 30-delta call (BXMD)

The 30-delta won the efficient frontier. Higher annualized return than the other two.

The mechanics:

🔹 Own the S&P 500.
🔹 Each month, sell 1 call priced at approximately 0.30 delta (further OTM, Black-Scholes determined).
🔹 The strike adapts to whatever implied vol is doing.
🔹 You collect less premium than the ATM version, but you keep enough upside that bull years aren't a drag.
